question: Your nightly Airflow DAG failed halfway through last night and got retried, and now the fact table has duplicate rows for that day. How did this happen and how do you fix it and prevent recurrence?
directAnswer: The root cause is a non-idempotent load task: it appends rows, so when the failed task retried after partially inserting, the retry inserted the same day's rows again, producing duplicates. The fix is to make the task idempotent, delete the day's partition (or MERGE on a key) before inserting, then clean up the current duplicates by rebuilding that partition. Prevention is idempotent design plus a unique test that would have failed the build immediately.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: This is a classic retry-plus-append data corruption. The task processed a data interval and used INSERT, so a partial run followed by a retry double-inserted the interval's rows because nothing scoped or de-duplicated the write.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Retries are enabled precisely so transient failures self-heal, but retries re-run the whole task. If the task's write is not idempotent, the second attempt compounds the first attempt's partial work instead of replacing it. The corruption is a direct consequence of pairing retries with a non-idempotent write.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: To fix now: identify the affected interval, then rebuild just that partition, either delete rows for that date and re-run the interval, or in dbt run --full-refresh scoped to the affected model if feasible. To prevent recurrence: change the load to delete-then-insert or MERGE on a unique_key so each interval is replaced, and add a unique/dbt test on the grain so any future duplication fails the pipeline instead of silently landing.

whyImportant: Duplicate-on-retry is one of the most common real production incidents, and interviewers want to see you both diagnose the idempotency root cause and lay out a concrete remediation-plus-prevention plan, not just delete the dupes and move on.
realWorldExample: The load task for July 2nd inserted 3 million of 5 million rows, hit a warehouse timeout, and Airflow retried it, inserting all 5 million again, leaving 8 million rows for the day. The engineer rebuilds July 2nd's partition via delete-then-insert, converts the task to MERGE on order_id, and adds a unique test on order_id so it can never happen unnoticed again.

nestedTopics.title: Diagnose via try_number and interval
nestedTopics.explanation: Airflow's task logs show the retry (try_number > 1) and the data interval. Correlating the retried interval with the day that has duplicates confirms the retry-plus-append cause rather than a source data issue.

nestedTopics.title: Fix: replace the partition
nestedTopics.explanation: Rather than trying to surgically delete only the duplicates, rebuild the whole affected interval idempotently: delete all rows for that date and re-run the interval, so the partition ends in a single correct copy regardless of prior partial state.

nestedTopics.title: Prevent: idempotent write plus grain test
nestedTopics.explanation: Convert the write to delete+insert or MERGE on a unique key so retries replace rather than append, and add a unique or unique_combination test on the grain so any duplication fails loudly instead of silently corrupting data.

followUps.question: Why not just deduplicate the table with a DISTINCT or row_number pass?
followUps.answer: Deduplicating after the fact treats the symptom, not the cause: the task will duplicate again on the next retry. It is also risky because rows may not be perfectly identical (a timestamp or load id may differ), making DISTINCT unreliable and row_number logic error-prone. The correct fix is to make the write idempotent so duplicates cannot occur, then rebuild the affected interval cleanly. A one-off dedup is at best a temporary patch while you deploy the real fix.

followUps.question: How would a dbt test have caught this earlier?
followUps.answer: A unique test (or dbt_utils.unique_combination_of_columns) on the table's grain compiles to a query that returns duplicate keys; if any exist, dbt build fails immediately after building that model, and it skips downstream models. So the duplication would have surfaced in the run that created it, blocking bad data from reaching marts and dashboards, instead of being discovered later by a confused analyst seeing inflated numbers.

followUps.question: What if the source itself can legitimately send updated versions of a row?
followUps.answer: Then append is definitely wrong and you need MERGE on the business key so an updated row overwrites the prior version rather than adding a second row. Configure the incremental model with a unique_key and the merge strategy, and use a lookback window so recently-updated rows are re-scanned. This handles both retries and legitimate updates with a single idempotent mechanism, keeping exactly one current row per key.

question: A stakeholder reports that a dashboard shows numbers off by exactly one day. Your Airflow DAG is scheduled @daily. What is likely wrong and how do you fix it?
directAnswer: This is the classic Airflow execution-date confusion: the code is probably filtering data by the current wall-clock date (datetime.now or today) instead of the run's data interval, or it misunderstands that a @daily run fires at the end of its interval. A run executing just after midnight on July 3rd is responsible for July 2nd's data interval. Fix it by filtering on data_interval_start/end (or ds) rather than the current date.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An off-by-one-day error where the pipeline processes or labels data for the wrong day. It stems from confusing wall-clock time with Airflow's logical data interval, which for a @daily DAG always lags real time by one interval.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Airflow deliberately runs a scheduled interval only after it completes, so the run for July 2nd starts at July 3rd 00:00. Engineers who filter on datetime.now() inside the task then grab July 3rd data (or none yet) instead of the July 2nd data the run represents, creating a consistent one-day skew.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The fix is to always derive date filters from the run context: use data_interval_start and data_interval_end (or the ds/ds_nodash macros for the logical date) to scope both the extraction and the dbt/SQL transformation. This ties every run deterministically to its interval, so the dashboard's day aligns with the data, and reruns/backfills also produce the correct day.

whyImportant: The execution-date model is Airflow's most notorious gotcha and a direct cause of subtle, embarrassing reporting bugs. Interviewers use this scenario to verify you truly understand end-of-interval scheduling and interval-scoped processing.
realWorldExample: A revenue DAG runs @daily at 00:15. The SQL filtered WHERE sale_date = current_date, so at 00:15 on July 3rd it grabbed July 3rd's (nearly empty) data and labeled the run July 3rd, while stakeholders expected July 2nd's completed totals. Switching the filter to WHERE sale_date = '{{ ds }}' (the logical date, July 2nd) fixed the one-day shift instantly.

nestedTopics.title: End-of-interval scheduling
nestedTopics.explanation: A @daily run for a given day executes after that day ends, so the physical run time is one interval ahead of the logical date. Any logic assuming run-time equals data-day will be off by one.

nestedTopics.title: Use ds / data_interval, never now()
nestedTopics.explanation: Filtering with datetime.now() or current_date couples processing to when the job happens to run, breaking on backfills and reruns. Deriving filters from ds or data_interval_start/end makes each run deterministic for its interval.

nestedTopics.title: Consistency across extract and transform
nestedTopics.explanation: The interval date must flow through the whole pipeline, extraction, load, and dbt, so every stage processes the same slice. Passing the interval date to dbt (via vars) keeps the transformation aligned with what Airflow extracted.

followUps.question: How do you pass the interval date from Airflow into a dbt run?
followUps.answer: Pass it as a dbt var: run dbt with --vars '{run_date: {{ ds }}}' (or the data_interval bounds) from the Airflow task, and have the incremental/model SQL filter on that var instead of current_date. This makes dbt process exactly the interval Airflow is responsible for, so extraction and transformation stay aligned and backfills of a given date produce that date's results deterministically.

followUps.question: Why does this bug often stay hidden until someone checks closely?
followUps.answer: Because every day is off by the same one day, totals still look plausible day to day; the pipeline runs green and nobody notices until a stakeholder reconciles a specific date against a source system. Consistent, systematic off-by-one errors are insidious precisely because they do not error out, they just quietly attribute data to the wrong day, which is why understanding the scheduling model up front matters so much.

followUps.question: How would you verify the fix across historical runs?
followUps.answer: Backfill or clear the affected date range so each run reprocesses with the corrected interval-based filter, then reconcile a few sample days against the source system to confirm the labels now match. Because the tasks should be idempotent and interval-scoped, replaying the range safely rewrites each day's data correctly. Adding a test that the max data date per run equals the run's logical date can also guard against regressions.

question: Your dbt project takes 3 hours to run and is blowing the warehouse budget. Walk through how you would diagnose and reduce cost and runtime.
directAnswer: Start by measuring: use dbt's run_results/timing and the warehouse query history to find the slowest and most expensive models, then attack the biggest offenders. The usual wins are converting full-rebuild tables to incremental models, fixing view models that are queried repeatedly, reducing unnecessary full-refreshes, pruning the DAG so only changed models run in CI, improving SQL (partition pruning, avoiding cross joins), and tuning warehouse sizing and clustering. Prioritize by cost times frequency.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: This is a performance and cost optimization exercise on a dbt project. The goal is to cut both wall-clock runtime and warehouse compute spend by targeting the models and patterns that dominate each.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: dbt runs entirely on warehouse compute, so inefficient models directly translate to money and time. As projects grow, full rebuilds of large tables and repeatedly-queried heavy views quietly balloon cost, and a scattershot approach wastes effort, so a measured, prioritized method is needed.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: First profile: dbt's artifacts (run_results.json) give per-model timing, and the warehouse's query history gives per-query cost/bytes scanned. Rank models by time and by cost times run frequency. Then remediate: make large append-heavy tables incremental so you process deltas not full history; turn heavy, frequently-queried views into tables to avoid recomputing on every read; scope CI runs with state:modified+ so only changed models and their children build; improve SQL to enable partition/cluster pruning and avoid exploding joins; and right-size or auto-suspend the warehouse.

whyImportant: Cost and runtime optimization is a high-value, frequently-tested skill because warehouse bills are a real business concern. Interviewers want a systematic, measure-first approach, not random tweaks, and evidence you understand the levers dbt and the warehouse provide.
realWorldExample: Profiling reveals one model, fct_events, rebuilds 40 billion rows every run, consuming 70% of runtime and cost. Converting it to an incremental model with a 2-day lookback merge cuts its runtime from 90 minutes to 6 and slashes its cost proportionally. Separately, three heavy staging views queried by many marts are switched to tables, removing repeated recomputation, taking the whole project from 3 hours to under 40 minutes.

nestedTopics.title: Measure before optimizing
nestedTopics.explanation: Use run_results.json timings and warehouse query history to rank models by runtime and by cost. Optimizing without data wastes effort on models that are not the bottleneck; the biggest cost times frequency items are where the wins are.

nestedTopics.title: Materialization and incrementalization
nestedTopics.explanation: Convert large full-rebuild tables to incremental to process only deltas, and reconsider whether heavy views should be tables (to avoid recompute on each read) or light tables should be views (to avoid needless builds). Materialization choice is the highest-leverage lever.

nestedTopics.title: Scope runs and tune the warehouse
nestedTopics.explanation: In CI use state:modified+ so only changed models and dependents build. In production, right-size the warehouse, enable auto-suspend, and use clustering/partitioning so queries prune data instead of scanning everything.

followUps.question: How do you decide which models to make incremental?
followUps.answer: Target large tables that mostly grow by appending (event logs, transactions) and are expensive to rebuild but cheap to update incrementally, especially those high on the cost-times-frequency ranking. Small tables and complex ones where most rows change each run gain little from incrementalization and add complexity (late-data handling, unique_key management). So incrementalize the big, append-dominant, expensive models first, and leave small or highly-mutable models as full rebuilds.

followUps.question: How does state:modified+ selection reduce CI cost?
followUps.answer: dbt can compare the current project to a stored manifest from a prior run and select only models that changed plus their downstream dependents (state:modified+). In CI this means a small change rebuilds only the affected subgraph instead of the entire project, cutting both runtime and warehouse spend dramatically on every pull request while still validating everything a change could affect.

followUps.question: What warehouse-side levers complement dbt-side optimization?
followUps.answer: Right-size the compute (a bigger warehouse can be cheaper if it finishes far faster, but avoid oversizing idle time), enable auto-suspend/auto-resume so you pay only while running, cluster or partition large tables on common filter columns so queries prune data, and separate workloads onto appropriately-sized warehouses. These warehouse-level settings, combined with dbt-side materialization and SQL improvements, address both the compute rate and the amount of work done.

question: An upstream source started loading late and inconsistently, so your downstream DAG sometimes runs on stale or incomplete data. How do you make the pipeline resilient?
directAnswer: Stop relying on a fixed time offset and make the downstream pipeline wait for data readiness. Add a source freshness check (dbt source freshness) or a sensor that verifies the expected data has landed before transforming, and ideally switch to data-aware scheduling so the downstream DAG triggers when the upstream actually finishes rather than at a guessed time. Combine this with alerting on staleness so late loads are visible rather than silently producing wrong results.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: This is making a consumer pipeline robust to an unreliable producer by gating execution on data readiness instead of clock time, and by detecting staleness explicitly rather than assuming the data is fresh.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Time-based coupling ('run at 3am, the load is usually done by then') breaks the moment the upstream is late or partial, and the failure is silent: the DAG runs successfully on stale data and publishes wrong numbers. Resilient pipelines exist to react to actual data availability and to fail loudly when data is not ready.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Declare freshness thresholds on the source (loaded_at_field, warn_after, error_after) and run dbt source freshness or a sensor first; if the source is stale, the pipeline waits, retries, or errors instead of proceeding. Better, use datasets/assets: the upstream marks its dataset updated on completion, and the downstream DAG is scheduled on that dataset so it runs only when the data is genuinely ready, regardless of how late that is. Alerts fire on freshness breaches so humans know.

whyImportant: Unreliable upstreams are a fact of life, and silently processing stale data erodes trust in the whole platform. Interviewers use this to see whether you design for data-readiness and observability rather than fragile timing assumptions.
realWorldExample: A partner file that used to land by 2am now sometimes arrives at 5am. The transform DAG ran at 3am and quietly produced incomplete reports. The team adds a sensor plus dbt source freshness that errors if the source is older than expected, and reschedules the transform on the upstream dataset so it only runs after the file lands, with a Slack alert if freshness is breached, so late data now delays the run instead of corrupting output.

nestedTopics.title: dbt source freshness
nestedTopics.explanation: Declaring loaded_at_field and warn_after/error_after lets dbt source freshness check how recent a source is. Running it as a gate means the pipeline can refuse to build on stale data and surface the staleness explicitly.

nestedTopics.title: Sensors and data-aware scheduling
nestedTopics.explanation: A sensor can wait for the file or partition to exist before transforming, and dataset/asset scheduling makes the downstream DAG trigger on actual upstream completion. Both replace fragile time offsets with real readiness signals.

nestedTopics.title: Alert on staleness, do not fail silently
nestedTopics.explanation: The worst outcome is a green run on stale data. Freshness breaches and readiness timeouts should raise alerts so the team knows the pipeline is waiting or the upstream is broken, turning a silent data-quality issue into a visible operational one.

followUps.question: Why is waiting for data readiness better than just running later?
followUps.answer: Pushing the schedule later only moves the guess; if the upstream is late by more than your new offset, you are back to processing stale data, and if it is early, you waste time waiting. Gating on readiness, via freshness checks, sensors, or dataset triggers, adapts to whenever the data actually lands, so the pipeline is correct whether the upstream is early or hours late, without repeated schedule tuning.

followUps.question: How do you prevent a readiness sensor from waiting forever?
followUps.answer: Set a timeout and a clear failure/alert path: if the data has not arrived within a reasonable window, the sensor should fail (or defer then fail) and trigger an alert so a human investigates the upstream, rather than silently blocking indefinitely. Use deferrable sensors so the wait does not consume worker slots, and consider an SLA or escalation so prolonged upstream lateness becomes a tracked incident instead of an invisible stall.

followUps.question: How does this scenario motivate moving from time-based to data-aware scheduling?
followUps.answer: The whole problem is that clock-based scheduling assumes data arrives on time, which unreliable upstreams violate. Data-aware (dataset/asset) scheduling expresses the true dependency, run when this data is produced, so the downstream fires exactly when the upstream finishes, however variable that is. It eliminates the brittle offset entirely and makes the dependency explicit and observable, which is why it is the recommended resilient pattern for coupled pipelines.

question: You need to backfill 18 months of a daily pipeline after fixing a transformation bug, without overwhelming the warehouse or breaking current daily runs. How do you approach it?
directAnswer: Plan a controlled, idempotent backfill rather than unleashing all 540 runs at once. First confirm every task is idempotent and interval-scoped so replaying a date safely overwrites it. Then run the backfill in bounded batches with strict concurrency limits (max_active_runs and pools) so the warehouse is not saturated, isolate it from the live daily schedule, monitor progress and cost, and validate a sample of backfilled dates against expectations before declaring it done.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A large historical reprocessing: rerunning 18 months of daily intervals through the corrected pipeline. The challenge is doing it correctly (each interval reproduced accurately) and safely (without resource exhaustion or disrupting ongoing production runs).
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Bug fixes that change transformation logic invalidate historical outputs, so you must reprocess history to make it consistent. But naive mass backfills spawn hundreds of concurrent runs that overwhelm the warehouse and starve the live daily pipeline, so a deliberate, paced approach is required.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Verify idempotency and interval-scoping so each rerun replaces its date's data. Trigger the backfill in batches (for example month by month) using airflow dags backfill or cleared task instances, capped by max_active_runs and a dedicated pool so only N intervals process at once. Keep the daily production run on its own schedule/pool so it is not blocked. Track cost and runtime, and after batches complete, reconcile spot-check dates against known-good numbers. For dbt, pass the interval date as a var so each model rebuilds the correct slice.

whyImportant: Large backfills are high-stakes operations that can rack up huge bills or take down a warehouse if done carelessly. Interviewers use this to assess operational judgment: idempotency, concurrency control, isolation, and validation.
realWorldExample: After fixing a currency-conversion bug, a team must reprocess 18 months. They backfill one month at a time with max_active_runs=4 and a warehouse pool of 4 slots, running on a separate, larger warehouse so the live daily job on its own warehouse is untouched. They watch cost per batch, and after each month reconcile a few dates against finance's figures before proceeding, finishing safely over a weekend.

nestedTopics.title: Idempotency is the precondition
nestedTopics.explanation: Every backfilled run must replace its interval's output (delete+insert or merge), not append. Without idempotency, reprocessing overlapping or previously-run dates corrupts data, so verifying idempotency is step zero of any backfill.

nestedTopics.title: Pace with concurrency controls
nestedTopics.explanation: max_active_runs caps concurrent DAG runs and pools cap tasks hitting a shared resource. Together they meter the backfill to a rate the warehouse can absorb, preventing the resource storm a naive all-at-once backfill causes.

nestedTopics.title: Isolate from and protect production
nestedTopics.explanation: Run the backfill on separate compute or a separate pool from the live daily pipeline, so the historical reprocessing does not delay or starve current runs. Batching and monitoring let you pause if cost or load spikes.

followUps.question: How do you keep the live daily pipeline running while backfilling months of history?
followUps.answer: Isolate the two workloads: give the backfill its own pool and, ideally, its own warehouse/compute so it competes with the daily run as little as possible, and cap the backfill's concurrency so it cannot monopolize shared resources. Because runs are interval-scoped and idempotent, the backfill of past dates and the daily run of the current date operate on different partitions and do not conflict. Monitoring lets you throttle the backfill if it starts to impact production latency.

followUps.question: How do you validate an 18-month backfill without checking every day?
followUps.answer: Use sampled and aggregate validation: reconcile a representative set of dates (month boundaries, known high-volume days, dates that exercised the bug) against a trusted source or prior known-good figures, and run aggregate checks like row counts and monthly totals across the whole range to spot anomalies. dbt tests on the rebuilt models (uniqueness, not-null, accepted ranges) provide automated coverage. This gives high confidence without manually inspecting all 540 days.

followUps.question: Would you use Airflow catchup or an explicit backfill command here, and why?
followUps.answer: An explicit, scoped backfill (or clearing specific runs) is safer than toggling catchup, because catchup can inadvertently schedule far more than intended and interacts with the live DAG's start_date. An explicit backfill lets you specify exactly the date range, run it in controlled batches with defined concurrency, and keep it separate from the normal schedule. Catchup is better suited to filling a small recent gap automatically, not a deliberate 18-month reprocessing that demands tight control.

question: A critical dbt model's test started failing in production, blocking downstream marts. Walk through how you triage and resolve it without shipping bad data.
directAnswer: First, understand the failure: identify which test failed and inspect the failing rows to see whether it is a real data problem or a too-strict test. Because dbt build already skipped downstream models on the failure, bad data has not propagated, so you have time. Decide whether to fix the data (fix the source/model and rerun), fix the test (if the assertion was wrong), or temporarily lower severity with a documented reason. Never blindly rerun until green.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A production data-quality incident triage: a dbt test failed, dbt build halted the affected subtree, and you must resolve the underlying issue and safely resume the marts without publishing incorrect data.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Tests exist to stop bad data, so a failing test is the system working as intended. The scenario tests your incident-handling discipline: diagnosing whether the data or the test is wrong, containing impact, and resolving root cause rather than muting the alarm.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Inspect the failing rows using dbt's store_failures results or by running the compiled test query. If it is a genuine data issue (a bad upstream load, a duplicate key), fix upstream and rerun the affected subtree with dbt build --select model+. If the test itself is wrong or overly strict, correct the test with justification. If it is a known, low-risk edge case blocking urgent delivery, you may temporarily set severity to warn with a documented ticket, but only as a stopgap. Downstream marts stay blocked until the node is healthy.

whyImportant: How an engineer handles a failing production test reveals their data-quality discipline. Interviewers watch for whether you investigate root cause and protect downstream consumers versus the anti-pattern of deleting or muting the test to make the pipeline green.
realWorldExample: A not_null test on customer_id in stg_orders fails, so dbt build skips fct_orders and the revenue marts. Inspecting failures shows an upstream loader started sending some rows with null ids after an API change. The team fixes the loader, reruns dbt build --select stg_orders+, the test passes, and the marts rebuild, all without the null-id rows ever reaching a dashboard.

nestedTopics.title: Inspect the failing rows first
nestedTopics.explanation: Use store_failures or the compiled test query to see exactly which rows violate the assertion. This tells you whether it is a real data defect, an upstream change, or a test that no longer matches reality, which drives the correct resolution.

nestedTopics.title: The build already contained the blast radius
nestedTopics.explanation: Because dbt build tests each node and skips dependents on failure, the bad data did not reach the marts. This containment buys time to fix root cause properly instead of racing to unblock, so resist reflexively forcing the run green.

nestedTopics.title: Fix data vs fix test vs adjust severity
nestedTopics.explanation: Choose deliberately: repair the data/source for genuine defects; correct the test if its assertion was wrong; or, only as a documented temporary measure, lower severity to warn for a known low-risk case. Silently deleting the test to unblock is the anti-pattern.

followUps.question: When is it acceptable to lower a test's severity to warn instead of fixing the data?
followUps.answer: Only as a deliberate, documented stopgap for a known, low-risk edge case where urgent delivery outweighs the residual risk, and with a tracked ticket to resolve it properly. For example, a handful of legitimately-null optional fields that a too-strict not_null flagged. It is never acceptable to silently mute or delete a test to make a genuine data defect disappear, because that ships bad data and destroys trust in the test suite.

followUps.question: How do you resume the downstream marts safely after fixing the issue?
followUps.answer: Rerun the affected subtree with node selection, for example dbt build --select failing_model+, so dbt rebuilds the fixed model, re-runs its tests, and only then builds the downstream marts that were previously skipped. Because the test now passes, the marts build on clean data. Verifying the test is green before the marts run guarantees you never republish on the bad data that caused the incident.

followUps.question: How would you prevent this class of failure from recurring?
followUps.answer: Address the root cause and add guardrails: if an upstream API change introduced nulls, add a source freshness/schema check or a contract on the source so such changes are caught at ingestion, and consider a model contract on the affected model to catch structural drift. Improving upstream monitoring and alerting means the next occurrence is caught earlier, and documenting the incident helps the team recognize the pattern. The goal is to shift detection upstream so the failure is prevented, not just re-caught.
